text: Faith: the old gods. A weirwood with a carved face stands on the village green.
Faith: the old gods. Weddings are made before the heart tree in the village grove.
Faith: the old gods. They pray before a heart tree in the wood above the fields.
Faith: the old gods. The heart tree here weeps red sap, and no one cuts wood near it.
Faith: the old gods. No priests and no temple, only an old weirwood by the spring.
Faith: the old gods. The nearest heart tree is a morning's walk away, in the lord's godswood.
Faith: the old gods. A carved weirwood stump marks where the village prays.
Faith: the Seven, as in White Harbor. A sept of white stone, small but proud.
Faith: the Seven, brought north by the Manderlys. A few old families still keep a heart tree.
Faith: the Seven. A septon from {DISTRICT} comes twice a year, when the roads allow.
Faith: the old gods, like the Blackwoods of Raventree. A weirwood stands at the village edge.
Faith: the old gods. Ravens roost in the village weirwood, as they do at Raventree.
Faith: the Seven, for the southron settlers. The black brothers pray at the sept of Castle Black.
Faith: the Seven and the old gods side by side; a weirwood and a wooden sept share the green.
Faith: the old gods. The free folk kneel to no king, only to the weirwoods of the haunted forest.
Faith: the old gods. They burn their dead, so that nothing walks again.
Faith: the old gods. Mainlanders whisper that the stoneborn still give blood to their weirwoods.
Faith: the old gods, kept the oldest way. A weirwood grove watches the bay.
Faith: the Seven. A seven-sided sept of stone, with its own septon and a bell.
Faith: the Seven. A stone sept with seven windows, the pride of the village.
Faith: the Seven. A septry of brown brothers nearby keeps bees, a mill and a brewhouse.
Faith: the Seven. A small wooden sept; a septon from {DISTRICT} comes on holy days.
Faith: the Seven. A roadside shrine bears the seven-pointed star; the sept is in {DISTRICT}.
Faith: the Seven. Begging brothers pass through and are fed at the sept door.
Faith: the Seven. No septon of its own: a wandering septon comes twice a year to marry and bless.
Faith: the Seven. The faithful walk to the sept in {DISTRICT} on holy days.
Faith: the Seven, though an old weirwood still stands nearby and some leave gifts there.
Faith: the Seven. A few old families still pray at a weirwood in the woods, as the First Men did.
Faith: the Seven. Lately men from Dragonstone speak of a red god, and the septon frowns.
Faith: the Drowned God. No temple: the drowned men baptise in the surf below the village.
Faith: the Drowned God. When a drowned priest comes with his driftwood cudgel, he is fed and housed.
Faith: the Drowned God. They give their dead to the sea and keep no idols.
Faith: the Seven. A domed sept of sandstone stands beside the village well.
Faith: the Seven. A small sept of sun-dried brick; a septon comes from {DISTRICT}.
Faith: the Seven. A wandering septon comes with the caravans, when they come.
Faith: the Seven, but the river folk still leave offerings to Mother Rhoyne.
Faith: the Seven. Orphans of the Greenblood moor here and sing to Mother Rhoyne at dusk.
Faith: many gods, as in Braavos. A shrine of the Moonsingers, who led the founders to the lagoon.
Faith: many gods. Some pray at the Moonsingers' shrine, others at the red priests' night fire.
Faith: many gods. In Braavos every god has a temple on the Isle of the Gods; here there is one shrine.
Faith: the many gods of Pentos. A field shrine; when harvests fail, they say the Prince will pay for it.
Faith: many gods. A red priest lights a night fire in {DISTRICT} for those who will listen.
Faith: the god of the bearded priests, whose name only initiates know. A bell calls the hours of prayer.
Faith: the nameless god of Norvos. A bearded priest in a hair shirt comes on holy days.
Faith: the god of the bearded priests. The village rises and rests by the bells of Norvos, as all must.
Faith: the Black Goat of Qohor. A calf or a kid is bled on the stone altar each holy day.
Faith: the Black Goat. The village sends a bullock to the temple when the priests ask.
Faith: the Black Goat. A blackened altar stone stands at the edge of the fields.
Faith: many gods, brought by freedmen from every land. The old maze-stones belong to none of them.
Faith: many gods. The cult of the Blind God is long dead, but its stone maze still stands.
Faith: no single faith, as in Myr. Shrines to many gods line the road; a red priest comes on market days.
Faith: many gods. The red temple of Myr takes a boy from the village now and then.
Faith: many gods. The old women keep a shrine to the Weeping Lady of Lys.
Faith: many gods. The love goddess of the Lyseni coins is honoured at every wedding.
Faith: many gods. A shrine of three-headed Trios stands at the edge of the village.
Faith: many gods. Red priests from Tyrosh preach in the market square.
Faith: many gods. The slaves turn to R'hllor, whose temple in Volantis is the greatest in the world.
Faith: many gods. A red priest, himself a slave of the temple, tends the night fire.
Faith: many gods. Men here fear the Fourteen Flames more than any of them.
Faith: the gods of Ghis, whose Graces keep the temples of the cities. The slaves pray in silence.
Faith: the gods of Ghis. A harpy carved over the shrine door watches who comes in.
Faith: the Great Shepherd. A mud-walled temple with a domed roof, sheepskins on the floor.
Faith: the Great Shepherd. All men are one flock, the godswife teaches.
Faith: many strange gods. Their temples crowd the waterfront of Qarth; here there is only a shrine.
Faith: the horse god of the Dothraki, for the riders. The village folk keep their own gods quietly.
Faith: the horse god. The riders say the first man came out of the Womb of the World.
Faith: the hundred gods of the Tall Men, honoured now only here and in Saath.
Faith: the gods of Ibben, whose priests sit among the Thousand.
Faith: the Lion of Night and the Maiden-Made-of-Light, parents of the God-on-Earth.
Faith: the god and goddess of love, beauty and fertility. The village keeps a temple of love.
Faith: the Great Shepherd. The temple is mud-walled and dark, with a blue-veined altar stone.
Faith: the Great Shepherd. A godswife tends the village temple and the sick alike.
Faith: the Seven. A small wooden sept with a white door, paid for by Manderly silver.
Faith: many gods. The magisters' gods have temples in Pentos; the village makes do with a roadside altar.
Faith: many gods. Every trader brings his own god to Myr, and some leave one behind in the village.
Faith: many gods. A red priest and a priestess of love share the village square on feast days.
Faith: many gods. The first head of Trios devours the dying, the village says, and the third gives them back.
Faith: many gods. The free keep the gods of their Valyrian fathers; the slaves keep the fire.
Faith: the gods of Ghis. The masters' household gods sit by the door, and the slaves bow as they pass.
Faith: many gods. Freedmen from every land each brought a god, and none of them quarrels.
Faith: the Seven. A sept of timber and daub, its seven-pointed star painted fresh every spring.
Faith: the Seven. Their septon is old and half deaf, and preaches mostly about the Stranger.
Faith: the Seven. Father, Mother, Warrior, Smith, Maiden, Crone and Stranger each have a candle in the sept.
Faith: the Seven. Women pray to the Mother in the sept, men to the Warrior and the Smith.
Faith: the old gods. Oaths are sworn before the heart tree, and no one breaks them lightly.
Faith: the old gods of the forest, nameless and countless, who watch through the weirwoods' eyes.
Faith: the nameless god of Norvos. At the hour of prayer the whole village stops work and kneels.
Faith: the god of the bearded priests. Men here go clean-shaven, for only priests may wear a beard.
Faith: the Black Goat. On holy days the god is given condemned men, and the village keeps out of trouble.
Faith: the Black Goat of Qohor, who must have blood every day.
Faith: many gods. Some here honour the Father of Waters, whose temple is rebuilt for each new bride.
Faith: many gods. A Westerosi sailor's widow keeps a little shrine of the Seven by the road.
Faith: the Seven. The sept is cool and dim inside, and the Mother's statue is veiled against the sun.
Faith: the Seven. As everywhere in Dorne, daughters inherit as sons do, and the septon blesses both.
Faith: the gods of Ghis. On holy days the masters ride to the temple of the Graces in the city.
Faith: many gods. At dusk the village gathers around the red priests' night fire to hear of the Lord of Light.
